title: Dance music of his boyhood: string bands, playing for nothing, and the family house
summary: He describes string bands and early orchestras, playing mandolin, guitar and bass for fun, and dances held in his father's old house.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught

blocks.x: Let's see, as the years go on here, sometimes the pay is going up a little bit too. There's more $6 dates here for some of the parties. Up to $6.25 quite often here. That's in the summer too. I'm wondering if you can tell us, Mr. Ballero, about the music when you first began playing. When you were a boy, before you joined any brass band, what was the dance music like here in Mobile? As far back as you can remember, did they have bands with blowing instruments or just strings? What kind of a band did they use?

Well, I think there were a few orchestras around there, but not really. The old time when the boys were coming up, they had most of what they called string bands. It would be string instruments with about maybe four, five, six pieces. But in the late years, after the Excelsior Band, well, during the Excelsior Band, about, I say about 20 years ago, they began to get orchestras together. The fellas began to organize good string orchestras, you see. They'd have pianos and trumpets and clarinet and violins and bass violins and all that. They had regular orchestras like they got now, you see. In my boyhood there, with most musicians around there, there wasn't much pay jobs, you see. It wasn't much pay jobs like it was in the late days where people could make some money out of giving dances and picnics. But in the early days, it was just almost, we'd have string bands and many times we'd go playing the way just to be playing for nothing, you see. Just to be playing for nothing. Yes, enjoy it. Have fun, get our beer and wine or something like that. And we'd play for nothing. And I'd borrow it there, because I'd play mandolin, I'd play guitar, bass, violin, and I could hit a tune on piano. And my wife's piano had been there for years. Well, I see you're moving in the piano. Yeah, she used to play the piano. Did your wife play for the dances too in the U.S.? Well, no, she never did go out for dances. She just played horn, yeah. And in this house, I guess it was around 80 some odd years old, and we had many dances in here with string music and brass music. Yeah, I was thinking, this tool on the chimney and having it relined it, you see. Oh, yes. The class began to fall after 80 some odd years. Yeah. And this was our father's house.
Well, I thought you were just maybe moving in here the way it's being reminded.
No, no, we had it relined it. We had it painted up a couple years ago all on the outside.
So you lived here for years? Yeah, yeah.

I see. And this is our father's homestead, our father's mother's homestead, my wife. And so this house, I guess, in its eight, it was close to 90 years. And all that lumber in there, solid, with the exception of the class, that began to get weak. And so it's having it all re-enined it now, you see. Yes. Putting solitaire at the top and sheetrock and putting that flow on it. This is as good and solid as this flow on top. Right now, that lumber is like a piece of oak under there. It's a pine lumber, you see.
